chapters.title: The Julio-Claudians and the Flavians
chapters.body:
Our image of the first century is largely Tacitus' image. Writing under Trajan, a senator who had prospered under Domitian and despised himself for it, Tacitus told the story of the Julio-Claudians as a progressive corruption of the governing class by autocracy: flattery, informers, treason trials, and the slow death of freedom of speech. Suetonius, an equestrian secretary of Hadrian, added biographies organised by rubric and full of gossip; Cassius Dio, a senator of the early third century, survives in excerpts for much of the period. The bias of these authors is senatorial, and the emperors who treated the Senate well (Augustus, Vespasian) fare better than those who did not. Inscriptions, papyri, coins and the documents of provincial administration correct this view by showing a system that functioned for the governed far more steadily than the court intrigues suggest.

[[tiberius|Tiberius]] (14-37), aged fifty-five at his accession, was an experienced general who wanted the Senate to share the burden of government, and was frustrated when it would not. Tacitus portrays him as a dissembler; the senatus consultum on the trial of Gnaeus Piso, found in Spain and published in 1996, shows the regime's own version of the crisis after the death of [[germanicus|Germanicus]] at Antioch in 19, and confirms Tacitus' facts while rejecting his tone. Germanicus' campaigns beyond the Rhine (14-16) recovered two of Varus' eagles but were then halted. The prosecutions for treason (maiestas) grew, fed by informers who received a share of the condemned man's property. Lucius Aelius Sejanus, praetorian prefect, concentrated the guard in a single camp on the Viminal (23), encouraged Tiberius' withdrawal to Capri (26-27), and eliminated the family of Germanicus, only to be destroyed by a letter read to the Senate on 18 October 31. A credit crisis in 33, triggered when the courts enforced an old law on investment in Italian land, was solved by an interest-free loan of 100 million sesterces from the treasury. Tiberius left 2,700 million sesterces in the treasury when he died in 37.

Gaius ([[caligula|Caligula]], 37-41), Germanicus' son, began with immense popularity and ended as a byword for cruelty and folly. The hostile sources on his madness are hard to disentangle from what may have been a deliberate humiliation of the Senate and a move towards open, Hellenistic-style monarchy. His order to set up his statue in the Temple at Jerusalem nearly provoked a revolt. He was murdered by praetorian officers on 24 January 41. While the Senate debated restoring the Republic, the guard found his uncle [[claudius|Claudius]] hiding in the palace and proclaimed him emperor; he paid each guardsman 15,000 sesterces, setting a precedent.

Claudius (41-54), scholarly and physically handicapped, was mocked by the sources as the tool of his wives and freedmen. In practice his reign was administratively active. Freedmen of the household headed the bureaus of correspondence (ab epistulis, Narcissus), finance (a rationibus, Pallas) and petitions (a libellis, Callistus), and procurators received jurisdiction in fiscal cases. He invaded Britain in 43 with four legions, built the new harbour at Portus, completed the Aqua Claudia and Anio Novus, and drained the Fucine lake. His speech of 48 urging the admission of Gallic nobles to the Senate survives in the original on the bronze Lyon tablet and in Tacitus' rewritten version, a rare chance to compare a historian with his source. His wife Messalina was executed in 48 after a public 'marriage' to Gaius Silius; his next wife, his niece Agrippina, secured the adoption of her son Nero over Claudius' own son Britannicus. Claudius died in 54, by all ancient accounts poisoned.

[[nero|Nero]] (54-68) succeeded at sixteen. The early years, guided by Seneca and the praetorian prefect Burrus, were remembered as good government (the 'quinquennium Neronis' of Trajan's alleged praise). Britannicus was poisoned in 55; Agrippina was murdered in 59. In Britain the revolt of [[boudica|Boudica]] (60 or 61) destroyed Camulodunum, Londinium and Verulamium before it was crushed. In the East the general Corbulo fought a long war with Parthia over Armenia, resolved by the compromise of Rhandeia, under which the Parthian prince Tiridates received his crown from Nero in Rome in 66. The Great Fire of July 64 destroyed three of Rome's fourteen regions and badly damaged seven. Nero rebuilt the city with wider streets and fire regulations and seized a vast area for his Golden House (Domus Aurea). To divert rumours that he had started the fire, he punished the Christians, the first imperial persecution (Tacitus, Annals 15.44). Financial pressure led to a reduction in the weight and fineness of the gold and silver coinage. The Pisonian conspiracy of 65 brought the deaths of Seneca and Lucan. Nero's tour of Greece in 66-67, competing in the games, alienated the elite further. The revolt of Vindex in Gaul (68) and the proclamation of Galba in Spain led the Senate to declare Nero a public enemy; he killed himself on 9 June 68, the last of the Julio-Claudians.

The year 69 revealed what Tacitus called the secret of empire: that an emperor could be made elsewhere than at Rome. [[galba|Galba]], an aged aristocrat, was murdered by the praetorians on 15 January in favour of [[otho|Otho]]; the Rhine legions proclaimed [[vitellius|Vitellius]], whose army defeated Otho at the first battle of Bedriacum near Cremona in April; Otho killed himself. The eastern and Danubian legions proclaimed [[vespasian|Vespasian]], commanding the war in Judaea, on 1 July at Alexandria. The Danubian army under Antonius Primus won the second battle of Bedriacum in October and sacked Cremona; in December the Capitol burned in street fighting and Vitellius was killed. At the same time the Batavian Julius Civilis led a revolt on the Rhine that grew into a short-lived 'empire of the Gauls'.

Vespasian (69-79), son of a tax collector from Reate, founded the Flavian dynasty on military victory and fiscal realism. A law conferring his powers survives in part (the lex de imperio Vespasiani), listing rights 'as Augustus, Tiberius and Claudius had'. He claimed that 40,000 million sesterces were needed to restore the state, raised taxes, sold imperial property, and famously defended a tax on urine collected for fullers by saying that money does not smell. His son [[titus|Titus]] took Jerusalem and destroyed the Temple in 70; the treasures carried in triumph appear on the Arch of Titus, and the Jewish temple tax was diverted to Jupiter Capitolinus. Vespasian and Titus held the censorship in 73-74, adlecting new senators from Italian towns and the western provinces, and granted Latin rights to all of Spain, after which the Flavian municipal charters (Malaca, Salpensa, Irni) organised hundreds of towns on a Roman model. Vespasian began the Flavian Amphitheatre on the site of Nero's private lake, a political statement in travertine.

Titus (79-81) reigned for barely two years, long enough for the eruption of Vesuvius (79), another great fire in Rome (80), and the inauguration of the Colosseum with 100 days of games. His brother [[domitian|Domitian]] (81-96) was an able and suspicious autocrat. He raised legionary pay by a third (from 225 to 300 denarii), restored the silver coinage for a time, fought the Chatti beyond the Rhine and the Dacians of [[decebalus|Decebalus]] on the Danube (85-89, ending in a compromise peace with subsidies), and recalled Agricola from Britain after Mons Graupius. He styled himself, the sources claim, 'lord and god' (dominus et deus), held the consulship seventeen times, and after the revolt of Antonius Saturninus at Mainz in January 89 turned increasingly against the Senate. The treason trials of 93-96 killed Stoic critics such as Helvidius Priscus and Arulenus Rusticus and even his cousin Flavius Clemens. He was murdered in a palace plot on 18 September 96, with the knowledge of his wife, and his memory was condemned.

Across eighty years the system had shown both fragility and resilience. Four emperors died by violence, one by suicide, and at least one, Claudius, probably by poison; there was a civil war, a fire, and two major provincial revolts. But the provinces were governed more predictably than under the Republic, the frontiers held, cities multiplied, and the administrative household of the emperor had become a permanent structure that operated whoever sat on the throne. The real constraint on an emperor was not law but the need to keep the soldiers paid and the elite in sufficient consent.
chapters.historiography: The central debate concerns how far to trust the senatorial tradition. Revisionist studies (Levick on Tiberius and Claudius, Griffin and Champlin on Nero, Jones on Domitian, Winterling on Caligula) read the hostile sources against documentary evidence and political logic, often presenting the 'bad' emperors as rulers who broke the Augustan conventions of civility (civilitas) with the Senate rather than as madmen. Wallace-Hadrill's 'civilis princeps' and Winterling's analysis of court society shaped this approach. The SC de Cn. Pisone patre, the Lyon tablet and the lex de imperio Vespasiani are key test cases for Tacitus' methods. The year 69 (Wellesley, Morgan) is studied for what it reveals about army loyalties and provincial identities.
reading: Levick, Tiberius the Politician (1976)
Levick, Claudius (1990)
Griffin, Nero: The End of a Dynasty (1984)
Champlin, Nero (2003)
Morgan, 69 AD: The Year of Four Emperors (2006)
Levick, Vespasian (1999)
Jones, The Emperor Domitian (1992)
Winterling, Caligula: A Biography (2011)

chapters.title: The High Empire
chapters.body:
Edward Gibbon famously judged the period from Domitian's death to the accession of Commodus the age in which the human race was most happy and prosperous. The judgement says as much about the Enlightenment as about the second century, but it captures something real: for most of these ninety-six years the empire was at peace internally, its frontiers expanded and then stabilised, its cities flourished, and its elite culture achieved a cosmopolitan confidence. It is also the age for which the narrative sources are worst: Tacitus ends in 96, Dio survives in Byzantine epitome, and the Historia Augusta, a collection of imperial biographies written around 400 by an anonymous author posing as six writers, mixes good information with outright fiction. Inscriptions, papyri, coins, legal texts and the literature of the Greek renaissance carry much of the weight.

The 'adoptive' system was an accident presented as a principle. [[nerva|Nerva]] (96-98), an elderly senator chosen by the conspirators against Domitian, faced a praetorian mutiny and secured his position by adopting [[trajan|Trajan]], the governor of Upper Germany, from a family of Italian settlers in Baetica. None of the next four emperors had a surviving son until Marcus Aurelius, so adoption of the best available man was as much necessity as ideology, though the Panegyricus of Pliny and later writers made a virtue of it.

Trajan (98-117), acclaimed 'Optimus Princeps', was the last great conqueror. In two [[dacian_wars|Dacian Wars]] (101-102 and 105-106) he crossed the Danube on Apollodorus of Damascus' bridge at Drobeta and destroyed the kingdom of Decebalus, whose treasure was said to be immense; Dacia became a province, colonised from across the empire, and the war is narrated in the spiral frieze of Trajan's Column (dedicated 113). Arabia (the Nabataean kingdom) was annexed in 106. Trajan's Forum, with the Basilica Ulpia and two libraries, was the grandest of the imperial fora. In Italy he funded alimenta, endowments whose interest supported poor children, recorded on bronze tablets at Veleia and among the Ligures Baebiani. Pliny's correspondence as governor of Bithynia-Pontus (around 110-112), including the famous exchange on Christians (Letters 10.96-97), shows Trajan's style: practical, legalistic and reluctant to encourage informers. His Parthian War (114-117) took Armenia, Mesopotamia and the Parthian capital Ctesiphon and reached the Persian Gulf, but revolts in the new provinces and a Jewish uprising in Cyrene, Egypt and Cyprus (115-117) undid much of it. He died in Cilicia in August 117.

[[hadrian|Hadrian]] (117-138), Trajan's cousin, announced an adoption that many doubted and immediately abandoned the eastern conquests. Four consulars were executed in his first year, souring his relations with the Senate. His reign was one of consolidation and inspection: he spent more than half of it travelling, visiting nearly every province, reviewing the troops (his address to the army at Lambaesis in 128 survives on stone) and building. The wall across northern Britain, begun in 122, and the palisade on the German frontier made visible the decision to stop expanding. In Greece he founded the Panhellenion and completed the Olympieion at Athens; in Rome he rebuilt the Pantheon and the temple of Venus and Roma; at Tibur he built a villa that was a miniature of the empire. His beloved Antinous drowned in the Nile in 130 and became a god. His plan to refound Jerusalem as the colony Aelia Capitolina helped provoke the revolt of Simon bar Kosiba (Bar Kokhba, 132-135/136), suppressed with great loss of life; Judaea was renamed Syria Palaestina. The jurist Salvius Julianus codified the praetor's edict (around 130), a milestone in Roman law.

[[antoninus_pius|Antoninus Pius]] (138-161) never left Italy. His long reign was peaceful except in Britain, where the frontier was briefly advanced to the Antonine Wall between Forth and Clyde (142), and in Mauretania. Aelius Aristides' Roman Oration (143 or 155) praised an empire of cities living in peace under a just ruler, the classic expression of provincial elite loyalty. The 900th anniversary of Rome was celebrated in 148.

[[marcus_aurelius|Marcus Aurelius]] (161-180) made his adoptive brother [[lucius_verus|Lucius Verus]] co-Augustus, the first collegial rule. Almost at once the Parthians invaded Armenia and Syria; Verus' generals, notably Avidius Cassius, took the offensive and sacked Seleucia and Ctesiphon (165). The returning army carried a pandemic, the 'Antonine plague', probably smallpox, which spread across the empire from 165-166 and recurred into the 180s. Its demographic impact is disputed: estimates of mortality range from under 10 to over 25 per cent, and papyri from Egypt show abandoned villages and a jump in wages and rents. Then the Marcomanni, Quadi and other peoples broke across the Danube (from 166/167), and in 170 a force reached Aquileia, the first invasion of Italy in nearly three centuries. Marcus spent most of his remaining years on campaign in the [[marcomannic_wars|Marcomannic Wars]], writing the private Stoic reflections we call the Meditations, and was planning new provinces north of the Danube when he died in 180. Avidius Cassius' revolt in the East in 175, after a false report of Marcus' death, collapsed within three months.

Marcus broke the adoptive pattern by elevating his son [[commodus|Commodus]] (co-emperor 177, sole 180-192). Commodus made peace on the Danube, returned to Rome, and left government to favourites: the praetorian prefect Perennis, lynched in 185, and the freedman Cleander, who sold offices (twenty-five consuls in one year, Dio says) until a grain riot brought his fall in 190. Commodus identified himself with Hercules, fought as a gladiator in the arena, renamed Rome after himself, and was strangled by a wrestler on New Year's Eve 192.

Beneath this narrative lay the society Gibbon admired. The empire held perhaps 60 to 75 million people. Hundreds of self-governing cities, each with its council of local landowners (decurions), magistrates and public buildings paid for by the competitive generosity of their elites, carried the burden of administration and tax collection. The Greek East experienced a cultural revival, the Second Sophistic, in which star orators such as Herodes Atticus, Dio of Prusa, Aelius Aristides and Polemo enjoyed imperial favour; Lucian satirised them, Galen practised medicine at court, Ptolemy wrote the Almagest, Plutarch and Arrian wrote history and biography in Greek. Senators from the eastern provinces became common. Trade flourished: Monte Testaccio in Rome is a hill of some 53 million broken olive-oil amphorae, mostly from Baetica, and the Muziris papyrus documents a single cargo from India worth nearly 7 million sesterces. Roman law spread with citizenship, and a legal distinction between the privileged (honestiores) and the humble (humiliores), with different punishments, hardened.

The prosperity was real but uneven, and it depended on peace that the reign of Marcus had shown to be fragile. Christianity, still a small minority, spread through the cities; the martyrdoms at Smyrna (Polycarp) and Lyon (177) show local hostility rather than systematic persecution. By 192 the empire faced war on two fronts, a weakened population, and a dynasty that had ended in murder. The next century would test whether the system could survive all three.
chapters.historiography: Gibbon's verdict has been both echoed and questioned: Rostovtzeff saw an urban bourgeoisie flourishing on an exploited peasantry; Garnsey and Saller analysed the economy, society and culture as an integrated system; Hopkins's 'taxes and trade' model argued that taxation drove monetisation and inter-regional exchange. The modern economic debate (the Cambridge Economic History; Scheidel, Temin, Bang, Wilson and Bowman) concerns the degree of growth, market integration and living standards. The Antonine plague is contested between maximalists (Duncan-Jones, Harper, who integrates climate change and disease) and minimalists (Bruun, Bagnall). On individual emperors Birley's biographies of Hadrian and Marcus are standard; the reliability of the Historia Augusta, exposed by Dessau in 1889 and mapped by Syme, governs much of the narrative.
reading: Garnsey and Saller, The Roman Empire: Economy, Society and Culture (2nd ed. 2014)
Birley, Hadrian: The Restless Emperor (1997)
Birley, Marcus Aurelius: A Biography (rev. ed. 1987)
Bennett, Trajan: Optimus Princeps (1997)
Scheidel, Morris and Saller (eds), The Cambridge Economic History of the Greco-Roman World (2007)
Harper, The Fate of Rome (2017)
Swain, Hellenism and Empire (1996)

chapters.title: Army, Frontiers and Provinces
chapters.body:
The empire of the Principate was governed by astonishingly few officials. Keith Hopkins estimated that around 150 senior administrators from the senatorial and equestrian orders ran an empire of 50 to 60 million people, about one for every 350,000 to 400,000 inhabitants, compared with one for every 15,000 or so in twelfth-century China. This was possible because the empire was a federation of self-governing cities supervised by governors, policed by an army stationed mostly on the frontiers, and taxed through local elites. Understanding these three elements, army, frontier and province, explains both the stability of the high empire and the strains of the third century.

The army that Augustus created numbered roughly 300,000 men, rising to perhaps 400,000 or more by the Severan period. A legion had about 5,000 to 5,500 heavy infantry in ten cohorts (the first of double strength from the later first century), with 120 horsemen, commanded by a senatorial legate, with six tribunes and sixty centurions. The auxiliary cohorts and cavalry alae, of 500 or 1,000 men recruited from non-citizens, roughly equalled the legions in number; on discharge after twenty-five years auxiliaries received citizenship for themselves and their children, recorded on bronze diplomas of which over a thousand survive. Pay rose from 225 denarii a year for a legionary under Augustus to 300 under Domitian, perhaps 450 under Septimius Severus and 675 under Caracalla, absorbing the largest share of the imperial budget; one estimate puts military costs at half or more of state expenditure. Recruitment shifted from Italians to provincials by the later first century and then increasingly to the frontier regions themselves, so that soldiers' sons, born in the settlements (canabae) outside fortresses, became the next generation of soldiers. Soldiers were forbidden to marry legally until Severus lifted the ban around 197, though many had unofficial families.

The writing tablets from Vindolanda, a fort just south of Hadrian's Wall, excavated since 1973, show the daily life of an auxiliary unit around AD 90-120: strength reports (of 752 men of the First Cohort of Tungrians, only 296 were present at Vindolanda on one day), requests for leave, accounts of beer and pepper, a birthday invitation from one officer's wife to another, and a dismissive note on the 'Brittunculi', the 'little Brits', who did not mount to throw javelins. The army was a bureaucracy as much as a fighting force.

Frontiers took different forms in different landscapes. On the Rhine and Danube, rivers patrolled by fleets and lined with fortresses (Vetera, Mogontiacum, Carnuntum, Aquincum) formed the core. Between the upper Rhine and Danube, the Upper German and Raetian limes ran some 550 km, a road and watchtowers reinforced under Hadrian with a timber palisade and later a ditch and bank or stone wall. In Britain, Hadrian's Wall ran 80 Roman miles (117 km) from the Tyne to the Solway, with milecastles, turrets, sixteen forts and a ditch behind (the Vallum) marking a military zone; the Antonine Wall, of turf, ran 60 km further north. In Africa ditches and walls (the Fossatum Africae) channelled the seasonal movement of pastoralists rather than blocking invaders. In the East, where Rome faced a state with comparable resources, the frontier ran along the Euphrates, later through northern Mesopotamia, defended by cities such as Dura-Europos and by client kingdoms until their annexation.

What were these frontiers for? Edward Luttwak's Grand Strategy of the Roman Empire (1976) argued that the empire moved from a hegemonic system of client states under the Julio-Claudians, to 'preclusive' defence of a fortified perimeter in the second century, to 'defence in depth' in the third and fourth. His work provoked a generation of critics. Benjamin Isaac and C. R. Whittaker argued that Roman frontiers were zones of interaction, not lines; that the army's tasks were internal policing and the projection of power as much as defence; that Rome lacked the maps, intelligence and planning apparatus to have a 'grand strategy' at all; and that the walls controlled movement and taxed trade more than they stopped armies. Susan Mattern showed that Roman decisions were shaped by honour, deterrence and the psychology of revenge. The likely truth is that emperors had consistent strategic habits without a doctrine: deterrence through overwhelming retaliation, the distribution of legions to where threats or rebellions were expected, and an aversion after Hadrian to costly conquest.

Provincial government combined the governor and the city. A senatorial governor, proconsul or legate, held jurisdiction, commanded troops if any, and toured his province holding assizes at major centres (conventus). His staff was small: a few officers, soldiers seconded as clerks and police, and his own household. Separately, equestrian procurators managed the emperor's properties and taxes. Smaller provinces, such as Judaea before 66 or Noricum, were governed by equestrian prefects or procurators. Direct taxes consisted of a land tax (tributum soli) and a poll tax (tributum capitis) assessed through periodic censuses; indirect taxes included customs dues (portoria, commonly 2.5 per cent at provincial boundaries, 25 per cent on the eastern frontier) and the 5 per cent inheritance tax on citizens. Cities were responsible for collecting much of this, and their councillors were liable for shortfalls, a burden that would grow heavier.

The cities themselves were the instruments of Romanisation. In the West, where urbanism was new, Rome founded colonies of veterans (Colchester, Cologne, Mérida, Timgad) and promoted native centres to the status of municipia with Latin rights, whose magistrates gained Roman citizenship on holding office. The bronze charter of the Flavian municipium of Irni in Baetica, found in 1981, preserves about two-thirds of a standard municipal law, regulating elections, councils, finances and lawsuits in astonishing detail. Local elites adopted Roman dress, houses, baths and Latin names, and competed for office. Whether this amounted to 'Romanisation', a term of Haverfield's era implying the spread of a superior culture, is now disputed: Greg Woolf described a process of 'becoming Roman' in which provincials actively chose and adapted Roman forms, while David Mattingly stressed the 'discrepant experiences' of different groups, from collaborating aristocrats to dispossessed peasants and enslaved miners. In the Greek East the cities were already old, and Roman rule worked through existing Hellenistic forms; Greek remained the language of administration there.

Citizenship expanded steadily, through military service, municipal office, manumission of slaves by citizen owners, and individual grants, until Caracalla's constitutio Antoniniana of 212 extended it to almost all free inhabitants. By then its legal value had diminished: what mattered in court was status as honestior or humilior. Resistance never disappeared. Major revolts in Pannonia (6-9), Germany (9), Africa (Tacfarinas, 17-24), Britain (Boudica, 60/61), Gaul and the Rhine (Civilis, 69-70) and Judaea (66-73 and 132-136) show where Roman rule was most resented: newly conquered regions with heavy demands and, in Judaea, a religious identity that imperial cult could not accommodate. But the more remarkable fact is how rarely the provinces rose once their elites had been integrated. The empire was held together less by its legions than by the interests of the landowning classes of a thousand cities.
chapters.historiography: Luttwak's thesis remains the reference point that critics define themselves against (Isaac, Whittaker, Mattern; Kagan's partial defence). Hopkins's 'taxes and trade' model and his estimates of administrative density inform debates about the weak state and the role of cities. On provincial culture, the debate has moved from Haverfield's Romanisation through Millett's elite-emulation model to Woolf's Becoming Roman and Mattingly's postcolonial critique, with growing attention to identity, religion and the countryside. Military studies have been transformed by documents (Vindolanda, Dura-Europos, Egyptian papyri, diplomas) and by archaeology of camps, frontiers and battlefields (Kalkriese, Harzhorn).
reading: Luttwak, The Grand Strategy of the Roman Empire (1976; rev. ed. 2016)
Isaac, The Limits of Empire: The Roman Army in the East (rev. ed. 1992)
Whittaker, Frontiers of the Roman Empire (1994)
Mattern, Rome and the Enemy (1999)
Campbell, The Emperor and the Roman Army 31 BC-AD 235 (1984)
Woolf, Becoming Roman (1998)
Mattingly, Imperialism, Power, and Identity (2011)
Bowman, Life and Letters on the Roman Frontier: Vindolanda and its People (1994)

chapters.title: The Severans and the Crisis of the Third Century
chapters.body:
The year 193 repeated 69. [[pertinax|Pertinax]], an elderly senator and son of a freedman, lasted eighty-seven days before the praetorians murdered him; they then auctioned the throne to [[didius_julianus|Didius Julianus]], who promised 25,000 sesterces a man. Three provincial armies proclaimed their own commanders: Pescennius Niger in Syria, Clodius Albinus in Britain, and [[septimius_severus|Lucius Septimius Severus]], an African senator from Lepcis Magna governing Upper Pannonia. Severus, nearest to Rome, marched on the city, had Julianus killed, dissolved the praetorian guard and replaced it with men from his Danubian legions. He defeated Niger at Issus (194) and, after taking Byzantium following a three-year siege, Albinus at Lugdunum (197) in a battle Dio says involved 150,000 men on each side.

Severus' reign (193-211) made the military foundation of imperial power explicit. He raised three new legions (I-III Parthica), stationing II Parthica at Albanum near Rome, the first legion in Italy for two centuries. He raised pay, allowed soldiers to marry, and opened promotions. He fought two Parthian wars, sacking Ctesiphon (197/198) and creating the province of Mesopotamia, and died at York in 211 during a campaign in Caledonia, reportedly advising his sons to agree with each other, enrich the soldiers and despise everyone else. The age was also the high point of Roman jurisprudence: Papinian, Ulpian and Paul, all praetorian prefects or high officials, wrote the works that make up much of Justinian's Digest.

[[caracalla|Caracalla]] (211-217) murdered his brother [[geta|Geta]] in their mother Julia Domna's arms. In 212 his edict (the constitutio Antoniniana) granted citizenship to nearly all free inhabitants of the empire; Dio cynically ascribed it to a wish to extend the inheritance tax. He introduced a new silver coin, the antoninianus (215), tariffed at two denarii but containing only about one and a half times the silver. Murdered near Carrhae in 217, he was succeeded by his praetorian prefect [[macrinus|Macrinus]], the first emperor not of senatorial rank, who was overthrown in 218 by the Syrian women of the Severan house in favour of the fourteen-year-old priest of the sun god of Emesa, [[elagabalus|Elagabalus]]. His religious innovations (the sacred stone of Elagabal installed in a new temple on the Palatine) and his conduct scandalised Rome; he was killed in 222 and replaced by his cousin [[severus_alexander|Severus Alexander]], under the guidance of his mother Julia Mamaea.

Two external changes now altered the strategic situation permanently. In 224 Ardashir, a Persian dynast from Fars, overthrew the last Arsacid king and founded the Sasanian empire, a more centralised and aggressive state that claimed the inheritance of the Achaemenids. And on the Rhine and Danube new confederations appeared: the Alamanni (first named in 213), the Franks (from the 250s) and, above all, the Goths, who by the 230s were established north of the Black Sea. When Severus Alexander, after an indecisive Persian campaign, tried to buy peace on the Rhine, his troops murdered him and his mother near Mainz in 235 and proclaimed the Thracian officer [[maximinus_thrax|Maximinus]].

The next fifty years saw around twenty emperors recognised at Rome and many more usurpers; nearly all died violently. In 238, the 'year of six emperors', a revolt of African landowners against Maximinus' tax collectors led to the proclamation of the Gordians, the Senate's own pair Pupienus and Balbinus, and finally the thirteen-year-old [[gordian_iii|Gordian III]]. The great Persian king [[shapur_i|Shapur I]] recorded his victories in a trilingual inscription at Naqsh-e Rostam (the Res Gestae Divi Saporis): Gordian killed at Misiche (244), with Philip ([[philip_the_arab|Philip the Arab]]) paying 500,000 denarii for peace; a Roman army of 60,000 destroyed at Barbalissos (252 or 253) and Antioch sacked; and in 260 the emperor [[valerian|Valerian]] himself captured near Edessa, the only Roman emperor taken alive by a foreign enemy, depicted kneeling on the rock reliefs. On the Danube the Goths under Cniva killed [[decius|Decius]] and his son at [[battle_of_abritus|Abritus]] in 251, the first emperor to die fighting a foreign enemy; Gothic and Herulian fleets raided the Aegean, burning the temple of Artemis at Ephesus (262) and Athens (267). The Juthungi reached Italy in 259-260; an altar found at Augsburg in 1992 celebrates their defeat and the liberation of thousands of Italian captives.

The empire fragmented. After Valerian's capture, the Rhine army proclaimed Postumus, who founded a 'Gallic Empire' with its own consuls and senate, ruling Gaul, Britain and for a time Spain (260-274), defending the Rhine rather than marching on Rome. In the East, Odaenathus of Palmyra destroyed the usurpers Macrianus and Quietus and drove the Persians back to Ctesiphon, acting as Rome's agent; after his murder (267) his widow [[zenobia|Zenobia]] ruled for her son Vaballathus, occupying Egypt and much of Asia Minor (270-272). [[gallienus|Gallienus]] (253-268), sole emperor from 260, held the centre, ended the persecution of Christians, and created a mobile cavalry force based at Milan. Aurelius Victor reports that he excluded senators from military command, completing a shift by which the army was run by career officers of equestrian rank, many from the Danubian provinces.

The economy was strained but not uniformly ruined. The silver content of the antoninianus fell from about 50 per cent under Caracalla to 2 to 5 per cent by 270; prices in Egypt, stable for two centuries, rose sharply after about 274. The state increasingly collected taxes in kind (the annona) to supply the army. Pestilence, the 'plague of Cyprian' (around 249-262), hit cities hard. In some regions, such as parts of Gaul and the Danube, villas were abandoned and towns contracted behind walls; others, like Africa, Egypt and much of the East, continued to prosper. Recent work has emphasised regional diversity over universal crisis.

Christians suffered the first empire-wide persecutions. Decius in 250 ordered all inhabitants to sacrifice and obtain a certificate (libellus), dozens of which survive on papyrus from Egypt. Valerian's edicts of 257-258 targeted clergy and property; Cyprian of Carthage and Pope Sixtus II were executed. The motive was the restoration of the gods' favour in an age of disaster, not hostility to an idea.

Recovery came from the Balkan officer class. [[claudius_gothicus|Claudius II]] (268-270) defeated the Goths at Naissus. [[aurelian|Aurelian]] (270-275), 'restorer of the world', drove invaders from Italy, began the 19-km brick wall around Rome, abandoned Dacia, defeated Zenobia at Immae and Emesa and took Palmyra (272), and accepted the surrender of the Gallic emperor Tetricus (274). He reformed the coinage, dedicated a temple to Sol Invictus on 25 December 274, and was murdered by his own officers in 275. [[probus|Probus]] (276-282) and Carus (282-283) continued the work. When Carus died at Ctesiphon and his son Numerian was found dead in his litter in 284, the army proclaimed a Dalmatian officer named Diocles. As Diocletian, he would rebuild the state on new foundations.
chapters.historiography: The 'crisis of the third century' was once an unquestioned category (Rostovtzeff saw a revolt of peasant soldiers against the urban bourgeoisie; Alföldi a general crisis). Since the 1990s scholars (Witschel, Liebeschuetz, Ando, Potter, Hekster) have questioned whether 'crisis' describes a period of diverse regional experiences and adaptive transformation, while others (Drinkwater, Harper) reaffirm a severe systemic shock driven by war on two fronts, epidemic disease and fiscal breakdown. The Sasanian sources (the ŠKZ inscription, Kartir's inscriptions) and numismatic and papyrological evidence for inflation have corrected the thin and unreliable Latin narrative (the Historia Augusta, Aurelius Victor, Eutropius, Zosimus, Dexippus' fragments, augmented by the Vienna Dexippus palimpsest published 2014).
